It fires strongest when the clause predicates something of a person (a personal pronoun, person noun or personal name - 'He was...', 'John Smith was the mayor...', 'Gerda Gilboe (1914-2009) was a Danish actress'), where auxiliary and passive be fire too, and stays below the active line for inanimate or abstract subjects, for plural are/were, for non-predicative as (comparative 'as good as', 'such as', 'as if', 'as soon as') and for directional or idiomatic into ('walked into the room', 'burst into tears', 'paid into an account').

Tide charts for the estuary had hung on the wall of the field station for thirty years, curling at the corners and fading where the afternoon sun reached them. Students came and went, filling notebooks with counts of shorebirds, salinity readings, and sketches of the mudflats at low water. Most of them remembered the same things about the place: the smell of the drying racks, the rattle of the old generator, and the way fog rolled in over the channel without any warning.

In the summer of 1998 a graduate student named Priya Raghunathan arrived with two duffel bags and a secondhand microscope. She had grown up inland, far from any coast, and had never seen a tidal flat before the morning she stepped off the ferry. The station manager, a taciturn man named Owen Ferris, handed her a clipboard and told her to start counting. For three weeks she worked the transects alone, rising before dawn and returning after dark, and by the end of that first month she could identify every common species in the mud without consulting a guide.

Her supervisor, Dr. Alina Reyes, was a pioneer of estuarine ecology, and she had spent two decades arguing that the small invertebrates at the base of the food web deserved serious attention, not only the charismatic birds that fed on them. Reyes had a reputation for bluntness. She once told a visiting committee that half the monitoring budget was wasted on equipment nobody knew how to calibrate, and the remark made the local paper. Priya, who had expected a legend, found instead a woman who arrived at the lab before six, made her own coffee, and read student drafts with a red pen in the margins.

The work was slow. The estuary was changing, and the older records were inconsistent. Some years the sampling had stopped in July; other years the sites had been moved after storms. Priya spent months rebuilding the chronology, matching handwritten logs to photographs, and corresponding with retired wardens who remembered details that no database contained. She learned that the mudflat she had studied all summer had once been a shipyard, and that the shipyard had closed after a fire in 1961.

By 2005 the station had a new roof and a working freezer. In 2006 Priya was awarded a small grant to hire two technicians. She published her first long paper on the recovery of the eelgrass beds, and the county began citing the station in its coastal planning documents. In 2009 she became the first permanent director of the field station, a title that came with a desk, a budget, and a great deal of paperwork. Today she is remembered by former students as a demanding but generous mentor, and she often told them that a good scientist must be patient with slow data. On the day she accepted the post she told the assembled staff that the station in 1998 had been a shed with a leaking roof, and that the credit belonged to the people who had kept the counts going through the lean years. Then she hung the faded tide charts above her desk.
